title: Photography direction for a fintech product
metaTitle: Fintech product website photography that proves
excerpt: Photograph the product in a real state and the people responsible for it. On a fintech site, pictures are part of the argument, not a mood under the headline.
alt: Yellow California poppies against a clear blue sky, a specific subject with nothing extra in the frame, for photography that should show the product rather than a vague mood.
caption: Poppies against a clear sky. A picture should be this sure of its subject. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should fintech website photos show?
faqs.answer: Show the product in a state a customer recognizes, and the people who are responsible for it. A payout list, a review queue, an operator at a real desk. Skip padlocks, handshakes, and city skylines that could belong to any company. The picture should support the sentence next to it.

faqs.question: Can we use stock photography on a fintech homepage?
faqs.answer: Use stock only when it shows a true situation and you are honest that it is not your office. A photograph of your actual product is better. A stock smile next to a claim about safety makes the claim look borrowed. If you cannot photograph the team yet, use the product interface and type, and wait.

faqs.question: How should we brief a photographer?
faqs.answer: Brief the scenes, not a mood board of blue gradients. List the product states, the people and their roles, and the rooms that are really yours. Say what to refuse: staged handshakes, cash fanned on a table, and laptops showing an interface you do not ship. Crop and caption are part of the brief.

markdown:
Fintech product website photography should show the product and the people responsible for it. A buyer who may trust you with money uses pictures as evidence. Abstract trust language, in words or in a photo of a padlock, fails that buyer.

The pictures are part of the argument, not a mood pasted under the headline. If the sentence says who reviews a hold, the photograph should be that work, or it should not be there.

## What the picture has to prove

Every photograph on the site should answer one of two questions. What does the product look like in a real state? Who is accountable for it? A picture that answers neither is scenery. Scenery is expensive on a page where the first seconds decide whether someone stays.

Google's guidance on how content is created points to evidence: what was done, and photographs of the work, not a claim standing alone. That advice is written about reviews. It fits a money product for a simpler reason. A reader is trying to see the thing they might rely on. A skyline, a marble lobby, or a handshake over a contract does not show a ledger. It shows that a brand deck had a finance section.

Decide the proof before you book the shoot. Write a list of frames the homepage, the about page, and one proof page actually need. Three strong pictures beat a library of almost. Wabisabi, a public Hanabi project, is a reminder that a calm, tactile world can still be specific. Calm is allowed. Vague is not. You can be quiet and still show the object.

Reject the category called "trust imagery" unless the frame contains your product or your people. Shields, locks, fingerprints, and anonymous suits are costumes. They reassure the team that the page looks serious. They tell a careful buyer the page is performing seriousness.

## The product in a real state

Photograph the interface, or compose it cleanly, in a state a customer could have. A payout that succeeded. A payout that failed and is visible. An export a finance lead would recognize. Empty states are allowed when they are honest empty states, designed on purpose, not a blank template with lorem balances.

Do not stage money as props. Stacks of cash, gold bars, and floating credit cards say "finance" to a stock search and say "this is not our product" to a buyer. If the product is a card, photograph the card you issue, in the material you ship, with the last digits treated the way your security note says you treat them. If you cannot show the card, show the app state that manages it.

Screens need a physical context only when the context adds a fact. An operator's desk with the queue on the screen says a person works this queue. A laptop on a marble island with a fake dashboard says advertising. Crop tight when the interface is the subject. Leave room when the person and the screen share the job.

Motion in a product film follows the same rule. A five-second loop of the real state changing is useful. A thirty-second anthem with a cursor flying through every menu is a delay. On the homepage, the still should be readable before any loop plays, and the loop should respect reduced motion. Hanabi treats reduced motion as part of the build, with Motion used where it clarifies, not where it introduces the brand.

## People who are responsible

Photograph the people whose roles you name on the about page. The operator who reviews exceptions. The founder who is the contact for a certain size of customer. The support lead. Put them in the room where that work happens, with the tools visible if the tools are not confidential.

Names and roles belong in the caption or the adjacent line, not only in a separate grid the reader might skip. A portrait without a responsibility is a yearbook. A responsibility without a real face is sometimes necessary, and then you should not fake the face. Use type.

Direction for the sitting: ask the person to do the job, or to pause inside it, rather than to smile at a lens they do not know. Candid, in this context, means occupied. It does not mean messy. A clean desk with a real queue is more persuasive than a laugh in a stairwell. Stairwell laughs can exist on a careers page. They should not carry the homepage claim about who answers.

Diverse, current, and consented. Do not reuse a teammate's photo from a different role after they have changed jobs. Do not photograph customers unless the story is approved. A customer quote under a stock photo of a different person is a factual error. On a financial topic, factual errors in the pictures count.

## What to refuse in the shot list

Write the refusals into the brief so they are not relitigated on set.

- Handshakes, especially over documents the camera cannot read.
- Padlocks, shields, keys, and fingerprints as the hero.
- Cash, coins, and piggy banks.
- City skylines and glass towers as a stand-in for the company.
- Models pretending to be your customers.
- Laptops showing a UI you do not ship, including a competitor's, including a generic dashboard kit.
- Dark hoodies in a server room as a picture of "security."

If a frame could be swapped onto another fintech site without anyone noticing, it does not belong on yours. The test is swapability. Specific beats atmospheric.

Also refuse pictures that contradict the copy. If you do not have a branch, do not photograph a banking hall. If a partner holds the funds, do not show a vault with your logo. The art direction has to obey the legal sentence. When they conflict, the sentence wins and the picture changes.

## Crop, color, and the caption

Crop to the proof. A wide shot is right when the room is the fact, as in a real operations desk. A tight shot is right when the product state is the fact. Do not leave half the frame to a plant because the layout has a hole. Change the layout.

Color grade toward the product, not toward a cinematic teal that makes the interface false. The UI in the photograph should match the UI in the browser. If you have to recolor the product to fit a campaign, you are no longer documenting it. Hanabi's design work starts in Figma and Illustrator and ends in the browser. The photograph should not invent a third palette.

Captions do the work the image cannot. "Failed payouts, reviewed by a person on the support desk" is a caption. "Our team, hard at work" is not. Write the caption when you select the frame, while the context is still known. A folder called "final-hero-v7" will not remember it.

WCAG 2, in the W3C overview, treats images as content that has to be perceivable, not only decorative. If the photograph carries the claim, the adjacent text must carry it too. Alt text describes the picture: who is in it, what is on the screen, what the room contains. Do not paste the keyword into the alt. Do not say "image of" and stop. A buyer using a screen reader should get the evidence, not a filename.

## A shot list you can hand to someone

A first shoot for this kind of site can be short.

1. One product state for the homepage, readable at phone width.
2. One wider frame of the same state with the responsible person.
3. A portrait of that person, or of two people if two roles share the job, with the role in the caption.
4. The room, only if the room is yours and adds a fact.
5. One detail that is true and specific: the export, the hold reason, the card, the paper form you actually use.
6. Nothing from the refuse list, even if the light is beautiful.

Give the photographer the product copy, not a mood adjective. "Trustworthy, modern, human" produces the pictures you just refused. "This is the hold queue. Please show it on Priya's screen, with Priya in the frame, no cash, no handshake" produces a picture you can publish.

Plan for the crop the layout needs. Homepage hero, a square for the about grid, a wide frame inside a proof page. Shoot those crops on purpose. A single landscape file will be ruined by three automatic crops that cut off the only part that mattered, the status on the payout.

If you are early and the team is small, do less. A clear product image and one real portrait outperform a rented office and a dozen stock frames. You can add pictures when there is more to show. You cannot easily recover from a homepage that taught the market your product is a handshake.

When you want a second opinion on the shot list before you spend the day, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the sentences the pictures are supposed to prove. The call should end with a shorter list, not a bigger mood board.

## After the files come back

Select by the argument, not by which frame is the most flattering. If the best smile loses the product, you do not have a hero yet. Ask for a reshoot of that one setup rather than compensating with type over a vague frame.

Name files by the scene and the version, and keep the approved crop with the caption in the same place as the brand files. On a Hanabi project that place is the client portal, with the other assets and docs, so the next page does not grab an unapproved outtake. Publish the version you meant. Retire the version that shows a dead UI.

Then look at the page with the pictures in it, on a phone, with the text removed in your mind. Do you still know what the company does and who is responsible? If the pictures only say "office" and "laptop," they are not done. The words may be carrying the whole decision. That is allowed for a week. It is not a photography direction.

The phone is where those pictures have to survive a smaller frame. [The mobile visit for a fintech product](/blog/the-mobile-visit-for-a-fintech-product) covers the first screen a buyer will actually judge, including which photograph still proves something when the crop gets tight.
